speaker: John Jumper
title: He won a Nobel here for AlphaFold. Then he left. - John Jumper
question: In 3D molecular deep learning, how much do hardcoded physical constraints and global rotational symmetries actually drive model accuracy in practice?
guest: It was important that we disrespected known symmetries of a protein. For example, atoms in a residue are separated by 1.3 angstroms, and in AlphaFold 1 we optimized them like a 900-joint robot arm. That geometry is really bad, so your optimizer has to take many steps. Breaking it up—treating residues as a residue gas initialized on top of each other—let refinement proceed in four or eight steps instead. We also used SE(3) equivariance, and people hooked onto it as the reason it worked. But in our ablations, AlphaFold 2 was about 30 GDT points better than AlphaFold 1, and removing equivariance only cost about two or two and a half points. Global SE(3) symmetry is not a very powerful symmetry in a messy real-world problem compared to things like permutation invariance or defining local reference frames for the loss. There are many ideas that added up to a transformative system—not one or two home runs, but eighteen doubles. We solved most problems two ways, so single ablations looked small, whereas turning off two redundant pieces together caused performance to crater.

points.note: Accept: torsion-angle or jointed robot-arm parameterizations making optimization ill-conditioned and forcing many gradient steps. Do not credit: generic claims that inductive biases reduce model capacity.

points.core: Relaxing physical geometry into unconstrained local frames lets the optimizer converge faster.
points.note: Accept: treating residues as independent unconstrained bodies ("residue gas") or violating bond lengths mid-network so refinement converges in far fewer steps. Do not credit: mentioning local coordinates without tying them to easier or faster optimization.

points.core: Global 3D rotational equivariance contributes only a small fraction of overall accuracy.
points.note: Accept: SE(3) equivariance being a relatively weak symmetry in messy real-world domains, or ablations showing only a minor accuracy drop when removed. Do not credit: claiming equivariance is the main driver of geometric deep learning success or both-sides hedging.

points.core: Transformative accuracy comes from stacking many small redundant improvements rather than one symmetry.
points.note: Accept: compounding many complementary architectural and loss wins ("eighteen doubles, not one home run") or redundant mechanisms where removing one barely hurts but removing two causes collapse. Do not credit: generic platitudes that "many factors matter."

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Less than the field long assumed, though they still matter in specific regimes. Hardcoded equivariance and physical priors (energy conservation, strict SO(3)/E(3) symmetry) deliver clear gains in data efficiency: models like NequIP and MACE reach strong accuracy with orders of magnitude less training data, and they give smoother, more stable molecular dynamics.

But at scale, the advantage shrinks. AlphaFold 3 dropped AlphaFold 2's equivariant structure module for a plain diffusion transformer with random rotation augmentation and got better. Non-equivariant or only loosely constrained models (Orb, Molecular Conformer Fields, and unconstrained transformers trained on large datasets such as OMol25) match or beat equivariant architectures on many benchmarks, learning approximate symmetry from data and augmentation while being faster and easier to scale.

The caveats are that learned symmetry is only approximate, and non-conservative force models (predicting forces directly rather than as energy gradients) can cause energy drift and failures in simulations, geometry optimisation and phonon calculations, even when test-set errors look excellent.

So the constraints act mainly as a useful inductive bias for small data and physical reliability, not as the primary driver of accuracy; data scale, model capacity and training recipe dominate.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
In practice, hardcoded rotational symmetries and physical constraints drive sample efficiency and simulation stability far more than peak static accuracy. When data is scarce, building exact E(3) or SE(3) equivariance into networks like NequIP or MACE substantially boosts generalization. At scale, however, unconstrained architectures trained with rotational data augmentation—such as AlphaFold 3’s raw-coordinate diffusion module and interatomic potentials like PET or Orb—routinely match or surpass strictly equivariant models on structure, energy, and force benchmarks, while running much faster by avoiding costly tensor products.

Still, the target application draws a critical line. Learned, approximate symmetry suffices for static structure prediction, generative design, and high-throughput screening. Conversely, in molecular dynamics, relaxing hardcoded physical laws—especially energy conservation, when predicting forces directly rather than as gradients of a scalar potential—causes spurious energy drift and broken thermodynamic observables despite low single-point force errors. Scale can substitute for architectural symmetry on static benchmarks, but explicit physical constraints remain essential for low-data regimes and physically faithful trajectories.

noweb.answer:
There’s no universal accuracy gain from hardcoding physics or rotational symmetry. Exact rotational symmetry tends to help most when training data are scarce, test orientations differ from training, or the model predicts vectors such as forces. It guarantees that a molecule’s predicted energy stays the same when the molecule rotates and that its predicted forces rotate with it. On standard benchmarks, models with strong geometric features and sufficient rotation augmentation can often narrow the accuracy gap.

Other physical constraints help when they address a failure that matters downstream. Deriving forces from a predicted energy guarantees conservative forces and can improve long molecular dynamics rollouts even when the change in test-set force error is small. In practice, the gain depends on the target, the data, and how the model will be used. Matched ablations and tests under rotations or on unfamiliar molecular configurations reveal more than a leaderboard comparison.
